Q: SELECT * except nth column A:

Good evening,

as many others before me I was looking for the SELECT * EXCLUDE pattern in Postgres.
Let's call it STAR-EX for simplicity below.
I came across discussions where this was requested (and rejected) even 15 years ago:

https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/flat/CAFj8pRAk14KEeSVrQUCGBhe4hiq%3DRDvt2yRqWGi4ZtrFLiJPCw%40mail.gmail.com#7b413b8875eb29863d13deb95eb784cb

Few points have been missing though and I like to share my perspective:

(1) The argumentation that STAR-EX is not SQL standard is true, but not compelling.
Languages have always been evolving and the fact that people ask for something over a period of at least 15 years should make us questioning the existing standard.
Likewise, STAR-EX is supported by more and more (esp. modern) databases such as Snowflake, BigQuery, DuckDB - some even with regex. Obviously, there is a need for this across several database communities.

(2) Then, it is mentioned that SELECT * and consequently STAR-EX would be bad design, because all columns should be listed for stability reasons. Personally, I find it difficult to call something "bad design" without knowing the respective application context.
What is bad design in one context, can be efficient and good design in a different context.
Sure it is bad practice for reasons of stability to use SELECT * on a source system object.
But in a multi-layered platform internal columns should not just suddenly change.

(3) The main advantage of STAR-EX (beside less redundant code in subselects) is way easier generic processing (e.g. using STAR-EX in procedures).
When we look beyond the individual pipeline or the ad-hoc analysis and consider procedures which run over hundreds (or thousands) of source/target objects with the same processing logic:
It can save a lot of effort to have a generic procedure solving the issue without knowing all columns in its many source objects. In fact, I would call that "DRY at its best" (dont-repeat-yourself) and certainly a good design.

Let's look at a concrete example:
A generic MERGE statement takes source and target as parameters, but noone would want to list the whole schema of the source. Then maybe 1 fixed column (lets call it JOB_ID here) should be excluded and added with a new value by the MERGE statement.
Creating views for all source objects is not feasible, because the number of objects can vary.
Creating views per execution (or even loop-run) was really inefficient and would put heavy load on the catalog for higher frequency of the statements.
Selecting all columns from the catalog and list the full schema (as recommended) can help as a work-around, but puts extra complexity on the code - and is still not efficient at runtime.

Particularly, as modern databases have this EXCLUDE feature, it could make a difference in database choice and platform design.

Completely agree that the EXCEPT keyword is not a good idea, as it would mix row filtering and column filtering.
But I do not see good reasons to not introduce the SELECT * EXCLUDE syntax in Postgres.

Q: Wordpress admin bar not showing on frontend A:

If the admin bar was shown, and WordPress has just been updated, a first step to try would be simply to log out of WordPress and log back in. That fixed it in my case.

I had just updated WordPress when the admin bar disappeared. A separate issue with WooCommerce and the REST API also unleashed itself. I tracked that down to a rest_cookie_invalid_nonce error (c.f. Payments settings tab greyed out – 403 Forbidden error on wc-admin/settings/paym and 403 Error in WordPress (WooCommerce) admin with multiple “sites”).

Logging out and back in fixed both issues.

It's worth checking in another browser to see if it might be a cookie issue. In my case the problems only exhibited themselves in Firefox (which I normally use) but not in Chrome. But as I was on localhost I did not want to delete all cookies there. I wish I had tried my suggestion here sooner - it would have saved a lot of time debugging.

Q: Jira Automation: Update Parent and Grandparent "Selected" Field When Child Issue Is Updated A:

I've made an automation such that

  • When work item is created or updated, with conditions of issuetype=story, task, and "parent" !=EMPTY

  • Then lookup work item (jql) - "parent" = {{triggerIssue.parent}}

  • Branch for parent

  • Then Edit work item field and set a custom field = {{lookupIssues.Story Points.sum}}

However I'm also looking for a way to update the grandparent item - made the more difficult because the instance played with the normal object hierarchy (epic is not immediately above story).
